corrections.before: A data race needs two accesses to the same memory, at least one a write, at the same time.
corrections.after: A data race involves conflicting accesses to the same memory, at least one a write, without the required happens-before ordering; exact definitions and atomic-access exceptions depend on the language. It does not require the accesses to occur at the same physical instant.

corrections.before: Shared named channels are CSP. In the actor model you send to an actor's address (its mailbox), not to a channel.
corrections.after: A channel does not grant direct access to another actor’s private state. The actor-model interface is an addressed message; a runtime may implement that interface with channels.

corrections.before: If thousands of unmatched messages accumulate, every such `receive` pays to scan them.
corrections.after: A fresh, unoptimized receive may scan thousands of unmatched messages before a match; fresh-reference optimizations and receive markers can avoid scanning older messages.

corrections.before: Under load, both occasionally crash with `timeout` errors at the same moment.
corrections.after: A trace shows Orders is handling a request and synchronously waiting for Stock, while Stock is handling another request and synchronously waiting for Orders; neither handler returns to its receive loop. The default call timeouts are unhandled.

corrections.before: Making one direction a `cast` (or having one server reply via a later message) breaks the cycle
corrections.after: Making one direction a `cast`, or deferring its reply and returning to the receive loop without waiting, breaks this waiting cycle

corrections.before: before 1.14 goroutines were only pre-empted at function calls
corrections.after: before 1.14 ordinary pre-emption relied on cooperative checks such as function prologues

corrections.before: Limiting how many operations run at once, for example with a semaphore of 100 or a fixed pool of workers, so a burst of work cannot exhaust connections, memory or the remote service.
corrections.after: Limiting how many operations occupy a protected stage at once, for example with a semaphore or worker pool. This can bound active requests, but tasks waiting outside that stage and retained data can still exhaust memory; a bounded backlog needs its own admission policy.

corrections.before: With `asyncio.Semaphore(100)`, at most 100 of 20,000 fetches are in flight at once.
corrections.after: With an asyncio.Semaphore(100) around each fetch, at most 100 fetches are inside that stage; 19,900 other scheduled tasks may still retain memory while waiting.

corrections.before: A threading model in which many user threads (M of them) all run on a single OS thread. Switching is cheap, but it cannot use more than one core and one blocking system call stalls every thread.
corrections.after: A threading model in which many user threads run on one OS thread. Those user threads cannot execute on multiple cores simultaneously. An unsupported blocking call can occupy their shared thread; runtime-aware operations can instead park a user task. Other OS threads in the process are a separate matter.

corrections.before: To set a thread or task aside, not runnable, until something it waits for happens, freeing the underlying OS thread for other work.
corrections.after: To make a task or thread temporarily non-runnable until a wakeup condition occurs. Parking a user-level task can free its carrier for other tasks; parking an OS thread frees CPU time but still retains that OS-thread resource.

corrections.before: In JavaScript, a value that counts as true in a condition. Every object, including any Promise, is truthy; only a few values such as `false`, `0`, `""`, `null` and `undefined` are falsy.
corrections.after: In JavaScript, a value converted to true in a condition. Ordinary objects, including every Promise, are truthy. Falsy values include false, numeric zero, the empty string, null, undefined and NaN; browsers also have the legacy document.all exception.

corrections.before: Erlang's `receive` behaviour: it scans the mailbox from the oldest message and takes the first one matching any of its patterns, leaving the others in place for later.
corrections.after: Erlang receive scans from the front of the message queue and removes the first matching message, leaving the rest. Ordinary messages retain per-sender arrival order, but OTP priority messages can be inserted ahead of ordinary traffic, so queue order is not always chronological arrival order.

corrections.before: OTP 28’s opt-in facility for messages sent through a priority-enabled process alias. Accepted priority messages enter the priority part of the queue ahead of ordinary messages while retaining order within each priority class; ordinary sender-signal ordering is a separate guarantee.
corrections.after: OTP 28’s opt-in priority-message facility, including explicit sends using a priority-enabled process alias and priority signals configured through links or monitors. Accepted priority messages enter the queue’s priority portion ahead of ordinary messages, preserving order within each class; signal arrival ordering is a separate guarantee.

corrections.before: An object standing for a result that will be available later, which can be waited on, polled or given callbacks. Java's `Future` and Scala's `Future` are examples; JavaScript calls the idea a Promise.
corrections.after: An object representing a result of work that may complete later. APIs differ: Java Future supports waiting, cancellation and status checks, while CompletionStage/CompletableFuture and Scala Future also support continuation callbacks. JavaScript calls its related abstraction a Promise.

corrections.before: Java's standard API for talking to relational databases. Its calls block the calling thread while the database responds.
corrections.after: Java’s standard API for accessing relational databases and related tabular data sources. Its ordinary query/update APIs are synchronous and may block the calling thread while a driver communicates with the database; metadata or cached operations need not perform a network wait.

corrections.before: How long a concurrent task exists, from being started to finishing or being cancelled. Unstructured spawns can outlive the code that started them; structured concurrency ties each task's lifetime to a block. (In Rust, lifetimes are also the compiler-checked spans for which references are valid.)
corrections.after: The interval from a concurrent task’s creation to its actual completion, including cancellation cleanup. A cancellation request does not itself end that interval. Unstructured spawns can outlive their caller; structured concurrency ties child completion to a scope. Rust reference lifetimes describe a different validity constraint.

corrections.before: A fixed number of workers that take jobs from a shared queue or channel and send back results, limiting how much runs at once.
corrections.after: A set of workers consuming jobs from a queue or channel. A configured worker bound limits how much work runs simultaneously; the queue needs its own capacity policy, and some pool implementations can vary their worker count.

significantCorrections: Bounded concurrency is not bounded retained memory: semaphore waiters still occupy task state; the glossary now agrees with the lesson’s bounded-backlog warning.
Actor timeout observations alone do not prove a cyclic wait. The question now gives an explicit two-handler wait trace, and the asynchronous fix explicitly returns to the receive loop.

Erlang selective receive removes the first matching message in queue order, which OTP priority insertion can distinguish from chronological arrival. Priority links and monitors are included alongside explicit alias sends.

Parking an OS thread consumes that thread resource; parking a user-level task can free its carrier. M:1 blocking wording now distinguishes supported cooperative operations from unsupported native calls.
Java Future does not expose continuation callbacks; the glossary distinguishes it from CompletableFuture/CompletionStage and Scala Future.
Corrected comments on the locked counter and released Rust guard so they describe the fixed operation; replaced stale whole-lesson numbers with descriptive short-unit references.
Data races need not occur at the same physical instant. Rust borrowing text now uses conflicting accesses and required ordering.
JavaScript ordinary objects and all Promises are truthy; the legacy browser document.all exception prevents an inaccurate universal-object definition.
Removed exact duplicate Further reading URLs while retaining each distinct source and all substantive lesson material.
